title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions and Other Matters Act, 2026

latest_action.text: Motion by Senator Schumer to reconsider, under the order of 10/9/2025, not having voted on the prevailing side, the vote by which the third cloture motion on the motion to proceed to S. 2882 was not invoked (Record Vote No. 557) entered in Senate.

official_summary:
Continuing Appropriations and Extensions and Other Matters Act, 2026

This bill provides continuing FY2026 appropriations for federal agencies, permanently extends the expanded premium tax credit for purchasing health insurance, provides additional funding for Medicaid and security for federal officials, and extends various expiring programs.

Specifically, the bill provides continuing FY2026 appropriations to federal agencies through the earlier of October 31, 2025, or the enactment of the applicable appropriations act. It is known as a continuing resolution (CR) and prevents a government shutdown that would otherwise occur if the FY2026 appropriations bills have not been enacted when FY2026 begins on October 1, 2025.

The CR funds most programs and activities at the FY2025 levels with several exceptions that provide funding flexibility and additional appropriations for various programs. For example, the CR provides additional funding for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and security for federal officials.

In addition, the CR

  • permanently extends provisions that expanded the premium tax credit, which generally reduces premiums for health insurance purchased through a health insurance exchange;
  • repeals health care provisions that were included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including provisions that reduced Medicaid funding; 
  • authorizes the District of Columbia to spend local funds at the rates included in its FY2026 local budget;
  • extends the availability of certain funds that are being withheld by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB); and
  • limits the authority of OMB to withhold appropriations.

Finally, the bill extends several expiring programs and authorities, including programs related to health care, veterans, homeland security, and agriculture.

summary.headline: Failed Senate bill would have funded the government through October 31, 2025, and permanently extended expanded health insurance tax credits.
summary.what_it_does: This bill would have kept federal agencies funded, mostly at 2025 levels, until October 31, 2025, or until full-year funding bills passed, to avoid a government shutdown. It would have permanently extended the larger tax credits that lower premiums for health plans bought through the insurance marketplaces. It would also have repealed health care parts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including Medicaid funding cuts, and limited the White House budget office's power to hold back money Congress had approved. It would have extended several expiring programs in health care, veterans' affairs, homeland security, and agriculture.

who_it_affects.how: Their agencies would have stayed funded through October 31, 2025, avoiding a shutdown during that time.

who_it_affects.group: People who buy health insurance through the marketplaces
who_it_affects.how: They would have kept the expanded premium tax credits permanently, which generally lower monthly premiums.
Medicaid funding cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act would have been reversed.
The Corporation for Public Broadcasting would have received additional funding.
Additional money would have gone toward their security.

who_it_affects.group: District of Columbia government and residents
who_it_affects.how: D.C. would have been allowed to spend its local funds at the levels in its 2026 local budget.

who_it_affects.group: Veterans, farmers, and users of other expiring programs
who_it_affects.how: Various health, veterans, homeland security, and agriculture programs would have been extended past their expiration dates.
